events.blurb: Dante completes the Divine Comedy, the journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise written in Tuscan Italian rather than Latin. It fixes the Italian language and makes a Florentine exile the judge of popes and emperors.
events.label: Dante completes the Comedy, c. 1320

events.blurb: Petrarch is crowned Poet Laureate in Rome, the first since antiquity. His recovery of Cicero's letters and his Italian lyrics make him the father of humanism.
events.label: Petrarch crowned laureate, 1341

events.blurb: Boccaccio completes the Decameron, one hundred tales told by young Florentines fleeing the Black Death. Its prose becomes a model for Italian literature.
events.label: Boccaccio, Decameron, c. 1353

events.blurb: The Byzantine scholar Manuel Chrysoloras begins teaching Greek in Florence, the first regular Greek instruction in western Europe for centuries. His pupils include the next generation of humanists.
events.label: Chrysoloras teaches Greek, 1397

events.blurb: Matteo Palmieri writes Della vita civile, a dialogue arguing that the good citizen serves the republic through public life. It is the clearest statement of Florentine civic humanism.
events.label: Palmieri, On Civic Life, 1429

events.blurb: Lorenzo Valla demonstrates, from the Latin itself, that the Donation of Constantine, the document by which the papacy claimed the western empire, is a forgery written centuries after Constantine's death.
events.label: Valla exposes the Donation, 1440

events.blurb: Marsilio Ficino's complete Latin Plato is published, the first translation of the whole surviving corpus. Under Medici patronage at Careggi, Ficino fuses Plato with Christianity into Neoplatonism.
events.label: Ficino's Plato published, 1484

events.blurb: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola writes his 900 Theses and the Oration on the Dignity of Man, arguing that humans, unlike angels or beasts, choose their own nature. The Oration becomes the manifesto of the Renaissance.
events.label: Pico's Oration, 1486

events.blurb: Aldus Manutius sets up his press in Venice, printing the Greek and Latin classics in small, affordable octavo volumes with italic type. The portable book spreads humanism beyond scholars to students and merchants.
events.label: Aldine Press founded, 1495

events.blurb: The Aldine Press publishes the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, a dream-romance of love and antiquity whose woodcuts and typography make it the most beautiful printed book of the Renaissance.
events.label: Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, 1499

events.blurb: In retirement after his arrest, Machiavelli writes The Prince, a handbook arguing that a ruler must learn how not to be good when necessity demands it. It circulates in manuscript for nineteen years before printing.
events.label: Machiavelli writes The Prince, 1513

events.blurb: Ludovico Ariosto publishes the first edition of Orlando Furioso, the chivalric epic that becomes Italy's national poem, mixing knights, magic, and irony.
events.label: Ariosto, Orlando Furioso, 1516

events.blurb: Machiavelli writes La Mandragola, a comedy of adultery and corruption in Florence that doubles as a portrait of a society that has lost its civic virtue.
events.label: Machiavelli, Mandragola, 1518

events.blurb: Baldassare Castiglione publishes The Book of the Courtier, the dialogue that defines the ideal courtier: educated, graceful, and concealing his effort under sprezzatura, studied nonchalance.
events.label: Castiglione, The Courtier, 1528

events.blurb: Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy are published posthumously, arguing the opposite case from The Prince: that republics, not princes, preserve liberty, and that Rome's tumults made it great.
events.label: Discourses published, 1531

events.blurb: The Prince is finally printed, five years after Machiavelli's death. The word Machiavellian enters the languages of Europe within a generation.
events.label: The Prince published, 1532

events.blurb: Giorgio Vasari publishes the Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, inventing art history: the story of art's rebirth from Giotto to Michelangelo.
events.label: Vasari, Lives of the Artists, 1550

events.blurb: Francesco Guicciardini's History of Italy is published posthumously, the great narrative of the Italian Wars by a man who served popes and Medici through them. It replaces chronicle with political analysis.
events.label: Guicciardini, History of Italy, 1561

events.blurb: Galileo publishes the Sidereus Nuncius, reporting what his telescope found: the Moon's mountains, the stars of the Milky Way, and four moons of Jupiter. Astronomy will never be the same.
events.label: Galileo, Starry Messenger, 1610

events.blurb: Galileo publishes the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, defending Copernicus in Italian for a general readership. The book's success forces the confrontation with the Inquisition.
events.label: Galileo, Dialogue, 1632

events.blurb: The Inquisition condemns Galileo, bans the Dialogue, and sentences him to house arrest for the rest of his life. He abjures, and the trial becomes the symbol of science against authority.
events.label: Galileo condemned, 1633
